newsitem.title: USA: G7 urges Ukraine to implement reform package.
newsitem.headline: G7 urges Ukraine to implement reform package.

text.p: The Group of Seven leading industrialized countries, irritated at Ukraine's inability to fulfil a bold package of IMF-backed reforms, said on Sunday that Kiev should adopt these policies before it was too late.
A statement released after a regular meeting of G7 finance ministers and central bank chiefs said the government needed to seize the window of opportunity for economic reform.

"We are increasingly concerned that the Ukrainian government has been unable to implement its ambitious reform agenda developed in cooperation with the IMF late last year for which the international community generously pledged its support in December," the strongly worded statement said.

"We urge the government to engage fully and quickly to implement this package while this window of opportunity remains open and before further delays make the reform task The G7 -- Britain, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and the United States -- was discussing the situation in Ukraine at a meeting where they stressed the need to avoid damaging shifts in exchange rate movements and expressed optimism about the outlook for economic growth.
The statement said Ukraine's unimplemented reform package had been designed to boost investment and bring a burgeoning shadow economy into the open.
"We consider these measures to be Ukraine's best chance to achieve positive, sustainable economic growth," it said.

Ukraine, independent since the Soviet Union fell apart at the end of 1991, has adopted a stop-go approach to economic reform, due in part to protracted wrangling between government and parliament and within the government itself.

The conservative-dominated parliament has not yet approved a budget for 1997 and while the International Monetary Fund says it made progress on talks this month, delays in the budget mean new IMF funding is on hold.
The new funding -- a $2.5-3 billion Extended Financing Facility to run for three years -- is part of a $5 billion loan package approved by international donors last December.

The money also included bilateral and World Bank loans, but release of the funds was conditional on the former Soviet republic pressing ahead with reforms, designed to transform the centrally planned system into a market economy modelled on that in the West.
